topics.title: Am, is, are: the verb be
topics.summary: Use am with I, is with he, she and it, and are with you, we and they.
topics.why: You need "be" in almost every sentence you say about yourself and other people.
rules: I am (I'm), you are (you're), he, she or it is (he's, she's, it's), we and they are.
Don't drop it: "She is a doctor", not "She a doctor"; "I am tired", not "I tired".
Negatives add not (I'm not, isn't, aren't); questions put it first: "Are you free?"

topics.title: Have and has
topics.summary: Use have with I, you, we and they, and has with he, she and it.
topics.why: You use it for family, things you own and plans: "I have a meeting at three."
rules: I, you, we and they have; he, she and it has: "She has two sisters."
Questions and negatives use do or does with have: "Do you have a pen?" "He doesn't have a car."
Don't say "I am having" when you mean own: "I have a laptop", not "I am having a laptop".

topics.title: A, an and the
topics.summary: Use "a" or "an" for one of many, and "the" when the listener knows which one.
topics.why: Articles are tiny, but missing them is one of the first things listeners notice.
rules: "a" before a consonant sound (a laptop, a university); "an" before a vowel sound (an app, an hour).

No article for general plurals and most place names: "Phones are expensive." "I live in Chennai."

topics.summary: Swap Indian-English habits like "passed out", "I have a doubt" and "discuss about" for what international listeners expect.

topics.title: Had done: the earlier past

topics.why: It makes your stories clear: "When I reached, the train had already left."

With before or after, the past simple is often enough: "After I ate, I left." Don't use had for everything.

topics.title: Could you tell me…? Polite questions
topics.summary: After "Could you tell me", "Do you know" or "I'd like to know", use normal word order: "where the bank is".
topics.why: Indirect questions sound polite in interviews, emails and at reception desks.
rules: Start politely: Could you tell me…? Do you know…? I was wondering…
Then use normal order, subject before verb: "Could you tell me where the lift is?", not "where is the lift?"
No do, does or did: "Do you know when the bus leaves?" For yes or no, use if: "Do you know if she's free?"

topics.title: However, although, because of
topics.summary: Although and because join sentences; despite and because of go before a noun; however starts a new sentence.
topics.why: Linking words make your answers sound organised and thoughtful.
rules: although or even though + a sentence: "Although I was nervous, I did well."
despite or because of + a noun: "Despite the rain, we went." "Because of the rain…"

rules: follow up (on something): check on it later. "I'll follow up on the invoice."
sort out means fix or organise; get back to someone means reply later.

topics.title: Question tags and soft questions
topics.summary: Match the tag to the sentence ("aren't you?", "doesn't she?") and soften big asks.
topics.why: Indian English often uses "no?" or "isn't it?" for every tag; matching tags sounds more natural.
rules: Positive sentence, negative tag: "You're from Kochi, aren't you?"
Negative sentence, positive tag: "It isn't too late, is it?"
